title: Privileged Process Integrity
summary: Privileged Process Integrity is the protection of the processes that already run with high trust, because an attacker who cannot obtain an administrator password will instead try to borrow the authority of a process that has one. The mechanism covers several related defences: restricting which identities may load code into another process, blocking the creation of remote threads, enforcing code integrity policy so only properly signed modules load, enabling exploit protections such as control flow integrity, and constraining debug and handle access that lets one process manipulate another. It also covers the way privileged services are configured, because a service that accepts an untrusted path, an unquoted binary path, or a writable directory in its loading order can be induced to run something else entirely. In real environments this appears as hardened service accounts, protected process settings for antivirus and authentication components, application control on drivers, restricted handle access, and monitoring for the process access behaviour that injection techniques require. Evidence includes process access and thread creation events, module load records, driver signature failures, and the service configuration changes that precede an escalation. The common misunderstandings are that antivirus products protect themselves automatically, and that injection is a rare exotic technique. Security software often needs explicit configuration to run protected, and process manipulation is a common step in commodity intrusions, not a specialist curiosity. A further misunderstanding is that kernel level protection is the only meaningful answer; many of the most valuable fixes are ordinary configuration hygiene around service paths, directory permissions, and who may debug a process.

beginner.definition: Some programs on a computer run with very high trust, such as security tools and login services. Privileged Process Integrity means protecting those programs from being changed or controlled by other software. The goal is to keep the trusted programs trustworthy.
beginner.whyItMatters: Attackers often cannot guess an administrator password, so they attack the software that already holds power. If they can attach to a security process, they can read secrets or switch off protection. These trusted programs also run early and stay running all day. Protecting them makes an attacker's job much harder and creates useful alerts.
howItWorks: Identify the processes that run with high rights, such as security agents and authentication services.
Limit which other programs may open, debug, or insert code into them.
Require that only properly signed drivers and system files may load into the operating system.
Check every service definition, and remove paths that point to folders a normal user can change.
Switch on exploit protections that make memory attacks harder and more likely to fail loudly.
Record attempts to reach those processes, because such attempts are rare and worth a look.
beginner.example: Think of a cash office inside a bank branch. The money is already inside, so a robber does not need the vault code. He only needs a way to reach the desk. The office therefore has a door that needs a special card. The glass shows every approach, and nobody may pass tools through the window. Privileged Process Integrity is that office design for the programs on your computer that already hold the keys.
takeaways: Attackers prefer to use the power that is already running rather than steal a password.
Check the paths inside service definitions, because a writable folder is an invitation.
Alert on attempts to debug or modify security processes, as legitimate software rarely does it.

objectives: Explain why privileged processes are targeted instead of administrator credentials.
Describe the controls that restrict code injection and cross process manipulation.
Identify service configuration weaknesses that allow escalation through a trusted program.
Explain how code integrity policy and driver signing protect the operating system.
Design monitoring that surfaces suspicious process access without drowning analysts.
